problem: Added 'by this admission'; dropped 'happened to be called'; added 'a man'; 'testimony/evidence' and 'without any further comment' reshaped.
replacement: While I was in America, a witness who happened to be called at the assizes of Chester County (State of New York) declared that he did not believe in the existence of God or in the immortality of the soul. The judge refused to admit his testimony, on the ground that the witness had destroyed in advance all the court’s confidence in what he was about to say. *e The newspapers reported the fact without any further comment.

problem: 'it must necessarily adopt maxims' lost 'necessarily' (force of the claim softened).
replacement: I am aware that at certain times religion may reinforce this influence, which originates in itself, with the artificial power of the laws and the support of the temporal institutions that direct society. Religions closely united to the governments of the earth have been known to exercise a sovereign authority drawn from the twofold source of terror and faith. But when a religion enters into an alliance of this kind, I do not hesitate to affirm that it makes the same mistake as a man who would sacrifice his future to his present welfare. In gaining a power to which it has no claim, it puts at risk the authority that is rightfully its own. When a religion founds its empire on the desire for immortality that lives in every human heart, it may aspire to universal dominion. But when it attaches itself to a government, it must necessarily adopt maxims that apply only to certain nations. Thus, by forming an alliance with a political power, religion increases its authority over a few and gives up the hope of reigning over all.

problem: 'political opponents' sharpened to 'political enemies'; 'allies of authority' softened to 'stand with authority'; 'reject' became 'turn against'.
replacement: Men today are not naturally in this condition with regard to religion. Some extraordinary or accidental cause must be at work in France, preventing the human mind from following its original tendencies and pushing it past the point where it would naturally stop. I am profoundly convinced that this extraordinary and accidental cause is the close tie between politics and religion. Europe’s unbelievers attack Christians as their political opponents rather than as their religious adversaries. They hate the Christian religion as the opinion of a party far more than as a mistaken belief, and they reject the clergy less because the clergy are the representatives of the Divinity than because they are the allies of authority.
